items.titel: «Génocide» des Rohingya en Birmanie: une décision historique attendue de la Cour internationale de justice
items.anriss: La Cour internationale de justice (CIJ), plus haute instance judiciaire de l'ONU, doit rendre ce jeudi 19 novembre sa décision sur les accusations de « génocide » visant la Birmanie pour les atrocités commises contre la minorité musulmane …

absaetze.t: La Cour internationale de justice (CIJ), plus haute instance judiciaire de l'ONU, doit rendre ce jeudi 19 novembre sa décision sur les accusations de « génocide » visant la Birmanie pour les atrocités commises contre la minorité musulmane des Rohingya en 2017. Un jugement particulièrement attendu, qui pourrait avoir des conséquences sur d'autres affaires examinées par la Cour, notamment celles concernant Gaza et l'Est de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC).
2 min Temps de lecture

En 2017, l'armée birmane avait mené des opérations dites de « nettoyage » dans l'État Rakhine (aussi appelé Arakan). Ces exactions avaient fait plus de 10 000 morts, entraîné la destruction de dizaines de villages et donné lieu à des violences sexuelles répétées contre les populations. Quelque 700 000 Rohingya avaient également fui vers le Bangladesh.

Saisie en 2019 par la Gambie, sur le fondement de la Convention de 1948 pour la prévention et la répression du crime de génocide, la Cour internationale de justice doit déterminer si la Birmanie est responsable d'un génocide. Cette juridiction juge les États, et non les individus.

Jusqu'à présent, la CIJ n'a jamais jugé un État responsable de génocide. Dans l'affaire des massacres de Srebrenica, en Bosnie, où 8 000 personnes avaient été tuées en 1995, elle avait reconnu qu'un génocide avait été commis, sans en attribuer la responsabilité à la Serbie.
Des conséquences possibles pour d'autres affaires

La décision attendue pourrait donc constituer une étape importante pour la justice internationale, comme l'explique Olivier Corten, professeur de droit international à Bruxelles. « Oui, c'est un moment très, très important. Tous les observateurs et observatrices sont particulièrement attentifs parce que, si la Cour décide qu'il y a eu un génocide, ça aura probablement, selon la motivation qu'elle va utiliser, pour conséquence que la notion va être, disons, envisagée de manière pas trop restrictive, pas trop stricte, et donc pourrait ensuite être utilisée dans d'autres affaires », explique-t-il.

Car il y a en effet d'autres affaires emblématiques en attente d'un jugement de la Cour internationale de justice. Parmi elles figure la plainte déposée en 2023 par l'Afrique du Sud contre Israël pour « génocide » dans la bande de Gaza.
La CIJ est également saisie d'une plainte de la République démocratique du Congo contre le Rwanda, déposée en 2026 pour des faits commis dans l'est du territoire congolais.

items.titel: Corée du Sud: la triche via les lunettes connectées perturbe l'examen d'entrée à l'université
items.anriss: Jeudi 19 novembre, plus de 550 000 lycéens sud-coréens passent leur examen d'entrée à l'université. Mais cette année, les lunettes connectées dotées d'intelligence artificielle (IA), capables d'afficher sur les verres les réponses du test, …

absaetze.t: Jeudi 19 novembre, plus de 550 000 lycéens sud-coréens passent leur examen d'entrée à l'université. Mais cette année, les lunettes connectées dotées d'intelligence artificielle (IA), capables d'afficher sur les verres les réponses du test, sèment la panique. Le risque de triche étant très important, le ministère de l'Éducation renforce sa surveillance mais semble démuni face à ces technologies. Les candidats, eux, tentent de montrer patte blanche.
2 min Temps de lecture
Avec notre correspondant à Séoul, Celio Fioretti

La suspicion est poussée à son maximum en Corée du Sud avant le Suneung, le grand examen d'entrée à l'université. Les candidats cherchent à faire preuve d'honnêteté avant de passer les épreuves. Ils ne veulent pas être accusés de tricherie à l'aide de lunettes connectées et dopées à l'IA. Quelques-uns vont même jusqu'à changer de lunettes, comme explique madame Choi, opticienne à Séoul : « Certains candidats vont jusqu'à remplacer leur monture épaisse par une monture plus fine, pour éviter tout malentendu. »

Le ministère de l'Éducation sud-coréen fait la chasse aux lunettes connectées, capables de donner des réponses aux tests aux personnes qui les portent. Du côté des professeurs, on ponte du doigt un manque de préparation pour repérer des appareils toujours plus discrets et plus petits, comme l'explique Kim Jaewon, professeur de lycée : « Les lunettes connectées se sont beaucoup allégées, et à l'œil nu, rien qu'en regardant les lunettes, il est difficile de les distinguer. »
Interdiction d'épreuve pendant dix ans

Ces lunettes ont déjà prouvé leur efficacité quand il s'agit de tricher. TechMong, Youtubeur coréen, l'a prouvé dans une vidéo devenue virale : « J'ai fait apprendre à l'IA les sujets des cinq dernières années. Pour les questions de 2026, je lui ai demandé de les résoudre lui-même. Après avoir corrigé du début à la fin, l'ordinateur n'a fait aucune faute ! »

La Première ministre, Han Seong-sook, a annoncé que les tricheurs seront punis pénalement et seront interdit d'épreuve pendant dix ans. Mais il reste impossible de se prémunir à 100% contre cette triche d'un nouveau genre qui pourrait bousculer les habitudes de l'éducation coréenne.

items.titel: What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from their Shenzhen meeting?
items.anriss: The US, Chinese and Russian leaders are to hold their first three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

absaetze.t: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a three-way meeting on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting on Thursday are arriving with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.
“It’s a summit of Trump’s ego, Putin’s tactics, China’s strategy,” Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.
So what does each leader want from this meeting?
What is this meeting about?

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Manila.

The White House has said that Trump plans to discuss the war with Iran as well as a possible three-way agreement on nuclear armament with Xi and Putin. Ukraine is not expected to be on the formal agenda, as Xi is understood to be reluctant to be drawn into what he views as a European matter.

The meeting comes as Trump has strained ties with traditional US allies, at times floating troop withdrawals from South Korea and cuts to assistance for Japan, while his administration continues to describe China as Washington’s main geopolitical rival.

Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at the Department of War Studies, King’s College, London, cautioned against viewing the summit as a new “carve-up” of the world order, however.

“It is a far cry from being a new Yalta,” he said. “In Yalta, you actually had the idea about how the world was going to look, and where the demarcation line would potentially be between the superpowers. We don’t have anything similar, not even the contours of that, in the making at this moment.”

At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to shape the post-war order, agreeing on the division of Germany and setting the stage for Soviet influence over Eastern Europe.
Where do China-Russia-US relations stand?
There are competing interests at play here.
US and China

Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, with Xi greeting him at the airport. This is their third in-person meeting since they paused their bitter trade war late last year. At its height, US trade tariffs on Chinese goods reached 145 percent, with China retaliating with tariffs of 125 percent on US goods, before a temporary truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, when tariffs were relaxed. Xi also agreed to pause new restrictions on exports of some rare earth metals which are crucial for manufacturing technology from smartphones to fighter jets. Soon after that, Trump relaxed restrictions on the sale of some Nvidia AI-related computer chips to China.
The truce has since been extended to January 10, 2027 to allow for broader trade talks.
Friction remains, however.
China’s rare earth mineral exports to the US are still about 75 percent below normal levels, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

A scandal over Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of US export controls, has also strained ties, as has the recent scandal over Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with a woman the US has accused of spying for China.
Beijing rejects all spying allegations as “baseless”, and Trump has said he does not plan to raise the issue at this meeting.
Expectations are low for a major thawing, however: Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, told Al Jazeera that a handshake without incident would be seen as a win.
US and Russia

Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, the first in direct format since February. The pair have visited both Kyiv and Moscow to promote these talks in recent days.
Days before they travelled to Moscow on Thursday last week, Trump said Washington and Moscow were close to a “big, beautiful agreement” covering not just Ukraine but “all of Europe”.

Trump’s rhetoric towards Putin has softened greatly in recent months, as it has hardened against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he has publicly admonished for targeting Russian energy facilities, driving up the global cost of oil and diesel. Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to step down and has paused some sanctions on Russian oil, much to the anger of many in his Republican Party.

Some analysts are concerned that US negotiators may offer Russia concessions on NATO in return for peace, including pushing a deal that allows Russia to retain land it has seized from Ukraine in the past four years – a prospect that alarms European leaders.
Russia and China
China has become Russia’s top trading partner since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, weeks after the two had declared a “no limits” partnership.
At a summit in Beijing in May this year, Xi and Putin signed more than 40 cooperation agreements and hailed growing energy trade.

Russian oil exports to China rose 35 percent in the first quarter of 2026, according to a Kremlin aide. China has also ignored Western demands to stop supplying high-tech components to Russia’s weapons industry.

Chinese President Xi Jinping called for China and Russia to “lead and advance the trend towards a multipolar world” after holding talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
The two leaders also met on Wednesday in Shenzhen.
Putin addressed the summit after Xi. He described Western powers as “former hegemons” and said Europe was experiencing a “humiliating decline”.
What does Trump want?
Analysts say Trump is the leader most eager to walk away with something he can present as a “win” from this trilateral meeting.

Vuksanovic said Trump is arriving “wounded domestically” following his Republican Party’s crushing defeat at the US midterm elections, which have seen the Democratic Party gain control of both US Houses of Congress. Trump’s legacy, Vuksanovic added, has been damaged by the war on Iran, particularly in light of Trump’s pledge not to drag the US into another “forever war” during his presidential campaign in 2024.
The deadlock that currently exists between the US and Iran has been described as a “frozen war” by observers.

“[Trump] hopes that he can get some quick-fix deal on something, at least, which he can then try to spin and sell to his base in the US as an enormous accomplishment,” Vuksanovic said. But he added that he doubts Trump could secure anything beyond “something very symbolic”, noting that the agenda of the meeting has remained opaque.

One issue Trump may push for is a trilateral agreement on nuclear armament. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) between Russia and the US lapsed in February. It was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. However, Xi is understood to be unenthusiastic about joining a treaty that China had no part in writing.

Lucas said Trump is there largely “for the photo opportunity”. But he drew a distinction between Trump and his administration, which he said wants to “regain their footing a little bit in terms of leadership” on China.

Washington’s China policy, Lucas said, has been “a disaster”. The administration launched a tariff war that saw duties climb as high as 145 percent, before Beijing retaliated by squeezing exports of rare earth minerals, forcing a truce.
“They’ve got to try to say: ‘Look, we’re leaders. Look, we have a firm policy on China, but one that’s not confrontational,'” he said.
That balancing act is complicated at home, Lucas added, with Republicans in Congress pushing for a tougher line on Beijing as the administration’s position weakens.
What does Putin want?
For Putin, the meeting is above all about the war in Ukraine and ending Russian isolation as a result of European and US sanctions.

“Putin and the Kremlin want cover for the invasion of Ukraine, because they’ve got some serious problems with it,” Lucas said. Moscow wants to keep the Trump camp on side, gain more Ukrainian territory and see Washington withdraw support for Kyiv, he added, while securing at least political backing from Beijing.

Lucas said Russia also wants to break “the notion that it’s isolated” after years of sanctions and the costs of a nearly five-year war that has not delivered victory. Putin is eager to prevent the US sanctions bill, which Trump has paused – and which would impose steep tariffs on Russia and on buyers of its goods, including China – from being implemented.

Vuksanovic said the optics alone, therefore, will be a prize for Moscow. After decades of complaining about US dominance, he said, Russia and China can now argue that “the power gap is not as great, so now we can sit at the table with the US”. That image of great-power status, he added, is “particularly appealing” to Putin.
Lucas added that Putin is unlikely to give up his leverage relating to Iran, and will resist offering Washington any binding promise that Moscow will not cooperate with Tehran.
What does Xi want?
For Xi, the host, the meeting is a chance to secure the space to pursue China’s long-term interests without interference.

“China wants the space to pursue its political, economic and military goals,” Lucas said. Beijing, he added, already has what it wanted in terms of recognition: “Now he’s on the same level with Trump and with Putin.”

What Beijing wants next, Lucas said, is no return to the tariff wars, no opposition to its alternative economic model, recognition of its primacy in rare earth minerals and technology, and no US pushback over Taiwan, which it regards as part of its territory.
China does not want anyone challenging its regional military presence, he said, including the Quad grouping of the US, Japan, India and Australia.

Vuksanovic described China as a rising superpower that is nevertheless “much more inward-looking” and focused on a vast process of internal reform. “They actually much rather prefer to be patient and to think long term, rather than to go for anything which is diplomatically grandiose,” he said.

He argued that China is “probably the biggest winner” of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have kept Washington distracted from the Asia Pacific. Beijing’s main worry, he said, is the risk of energy markets collapsing.
“Minus that economic risk, they’re still happy that the US is bogged down in two major wars which Washington does not know how to disentangle itself from,” he said.
Will this meeting change anything on Iran or Ukraine?
Observers are not expecting any sort of a breakthrough from this meeting.

On Iran, Lucas said the US administration would like Beijing to “privately urge the Iranians to make compromises”. But US-Iran talks remain stuck on whether to address the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran first, or its nuclear programme.

Vuksanovic said he is “very dubious” that China would take on a major mediating role. Beyond brokering the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023, he said, Beijing has preferred to be “diplomatically skilful rhetorically, without sticking out as a major conflict mediator”.

items.titel: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
items.anriss: The Gambia accuses Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown that displaced at least 730,000 Rohingya.

absaetze.t: The Gambia accused Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown displacing over 730,000 Rohingya.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.
The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.
It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.
What is the case?
The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.
Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.
Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.
Why is it significant?
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.
The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.

The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely. Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.

items.titel: US surges power projection to westernmost island chain as Russia, China loom
items.anriss: The U.S. Air Force is stepping up its training on the country’s westernmost islands as it seeks to develop more places from which to project power and monitor adversaries across the Pacific and the Arctic.

absaetze.t: The U.S. Air Force is stepping up its training on the country’s westernmost islands as it seeks to develop more places from which to project power and monitor adversaries across the Pacific and the Arctic.

Those efforts were visible in late October, when airmen deployed to Shemya Island in Alaska’s Aleutian Islands for a rare exercise, and when the Air Force released a proposal outlining its plans for operations on islands near Guam.

On Shemya, which is closer to Russia than to mainland Alaska, F-16s, tankers and cargo planes deployed to Eareckson Air Station from Oct. 18 to Oct. 26. While there, the jets “sat alert,” with crews in position and maintaining readiness to launch on short notice.

“While it was commonplace for aircraft to sit alert in the 1980s, this deployment marks the first time in decades that aircraft have sat alert at Eareckson,” Capt. Kitsana Dounglomchan, Alaskan NORAD Region spokesperson, said in an email.

The Shemya deployment ended with long-range operations as part of a U.S.-Canada homeland-defense exercise. As F-16s launched from Eareckson to cover the southern portion of the Alaska theater of operations, F-35s and F-16s at Eielson Air Force Base 1,600 miles to the west took off to cover the northwest portion of the theater. Canadian CF-18s flew from their base at Cold Lake, 2,600 miles from Shemya, to cover the northern part.

Operating from Eareckson “proved we can deploy to an austere location, maintain alert, launch on short notice, and seamlessly integrate U.S. and Canadian forces to defend the northern approaches,” Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of the Alaskan NORAD region, said in a press release.

The U.S. military has been active on Shemya since World War II. During the Cold War, the base hosted refueling and surveillance aircraft as well as radars to monitor Soviet activity, especially Soviet ICBMs. The massive Cobra Dane radar was built there in the 1970s and is still used to monitor missile activity.

Recent deployments to Shemya underscore its continued relevance as a perch in the Aleutians, which stretch across strategically important waters linking the Pacific and Arctic. A “force projection operation” by U.S. soldiers with HIMARS launchers in September 2024 came after a flurry of Russian and Chinese activity in the area, including the first Sino-Russian bomber patrol near Alaska. Other recent exercises appear to have focused on defending the island’s infrastructure from seaborne incursions and aerial attacks.

While at Eareckson, airmen also certified the base’s aircraft-arresting system to handle F-16s, “further validating Eareckson Air Station as a viable location for future fighter operations from an austere airfield,” according to a press release. Dounglomchan declined to comment on future operations at Eareckson but said NORAD maintains “the operational capability” to move forces around Alaska and the Arctic “at a time and place of our choosing” and “oftentimes to remote locations like Eareckson.”

As the drills on Shemya wrapped up, the Air Force shared its plans for future operations on islands in the central Pacific. In a proposal released at the end of October, the service said it would study the impact of conducting up to 1,500 and potentially more than 1,800 aircraft operations, such as takeoffs and landings, annually at airfields on Rota, Saipan, and Tinian in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

The operations would be part of small, medium and large drills held several times a year for a few weeks at a time. They would also involve deployment of up to 550,000 gallons of fuel and up to 1,000 personnel at each airfield, as well as munitions, temporary infrastructure, and support operations. The Air Force said its study would assess “the potential social, economic, and environmental effects” of those operations.

The study won’t be completed until mid-2028, but the proposal highlights the Air Force’s recent focus on those islands, especially Tinian, where airmen are refurbishing North Field, one of the U.S.’s largest and most important WWII airbases. North Field was abandoned and overgrown after the war, but airmen have been clearing vegetation, removing debris and rehabilitating runways since late 2023.
That work is ongoing but had progressed enough by mid-2025 for North Field to be deemed “a semi-permanent [contingency] location” for the Air Force’s main base on Guam, about 100 miles to the south.

The Northern Marianas is a U.S. territory in the Second Island Chain, which stretches from Japan through the central Pacific to Indonesia. The Air Force has been scouting airfields in that island chain and conducting renovations and upgrades to make them better able to support its Agile Combat Employment concept, which emphasizes dispersal and resilience to counter the threat from China.

“China’s missile force is large, but it’s not unlimited. Every additional airfield from where the Air Force can operate is another of targets China has to cover. That’s the logic behind Agile Combat Employment,” said Kelly Greico, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Improvements on Shemya and in the Northern Marianas enhance the Air Force’s ability to operate in those places, but those operations are influenced by the islands’ locations, according to Greico, whose research focuses on airpower strategy.

Shemya “is primarily about homeland defense. Its location in the North Pacific makes it useful mainly as a forward operating location for NORAD,” Greico said. “The value of the remote airfield lies less in its ability to generate sorties under contested conditions than in its geographic position in intercepting Russian aircraft forward.”

But investments in Rota, Tinian, and Saipan, Greico added, “are primarily about expanding the number of locations from which the Air Force could operate, reducing its dependence on Andersen Air Base at Guam.”

Both Shemya and the Northern Marianas provide the benefit of being U.S. territory, giving the Pentagon greater freedom to operate. Bases in the Philippines and Japan are closer to China, but those countries have more control over what U.S. forces do at their facilities and may limit their access and operations during a crisis or conflict.

Geography tempers those political benefits, however. In the Stimson Center’s modeling, dispersal had “the biggest effect of any countermeasure we tested,” Greico said. “But the effect is much smaller in the Second Island Chain than in Japan, because there just aren’t many runways out there.”

“Chinese missile strikes could keep U.S. runways in Guam and other Pacific islands closed to tankers and bombers for about four days. Adding civilian airfields in Guam, the Northern Marianas, and Palau only reduced those times by a matter of hours,” Greico added. “Geography matters here. There’s a lot of water out there, but not much land.”

items.titel: Tehran Widens Attacks On Gulf Nations After Latest U.S. Strike On Iranian Island

absaetze.t: Amid stalled efforts to find a diplomatic solution to the conflict between the U.S. and Iran, the Islamic Republic is stepping up attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain, two nations that host American bases. Wednesday’s strikes took place after the latest U.S. attack on Iran’s Qeshm Island.
These actions, along with other developments we will discuss below, raise questions about whether the Middle East could erupt into a new round of intense fighting.
New Iranian Attacks On Gulf Nations

On Wednesday, Kuwait and Bahrain said they both intercepted Iranian strikes. For Kuwait, it was the first time since September it had been attacked. The strikes on Bahrain marked a continuation of Iranian attacks that began Nov. 13 after they had been paused for two months.

These strikes appear to be an escalation of Iranian actions in response to a U.S. attack on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, The Associated Press suggested. We will discuss that in more detail later in this story.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently countering hostile drone attacks,” the Kuwaiti Army posted on X early Wednesday morning local time. “The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defense systems intercepting hostile attacks. Everyone is requested to comply with the security and safety instructions issued by the relevant authorities.”

The Iranian Army claimed that “its combat drones have targeted Patriot air defense systems and drone and missile launch platforms at the US Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait early Wednesday,” according to the Iranian Tasnim news agency affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Tasnim offered no visual proof of an attack on Ali Al-Salem Air Base and none has emerged so far on social media either. Iran has frequently made claims that proved to be false about successful attacks on U.S. assets.
As we noted earlier, Bahrain also said it came under Iranian fire.

“The General Command of the Bahrain Defense Force announces that Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its vicious attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain,” the Bahrain Defense Force (BDF) stated on Instagram. “The General Command confirms that with a firm will and high combat readiness, the air defense systems of the Bahrain Defense Force (BDF) responded to a number of Iranian air attacks on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.”
The BDF did not say whether it repelled Iranian missiles or drones, and there was no immediate Iranian claim that it targeted Bahrain on Wednesday.
A day earlier, the IRGC claimed it hit a radar system at a base in Bahrain. CENTCOM quickly disputed that claim.

Wednesday’s Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain sparked unconfirmed speculation among open-source flight trackers that a C-17 Globemaster III transport jet, coded as a medical evacuation flight, may have been carrying wounded U.S. troops. The flight left the Middle East headed for Ramstein Air Base in Germany, which is located near Landstuhl Regional Medical Center, where many wounded troops are first sent before heading home.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) put out a message on X Wednesday afternoon saying no troops were injured.
Earlier, a U.S. official told us there had been “zero impacts” on U.S. facilities in the region from Iranian attacks despite several recent claims out of Tehran.
To date, 23 U.S. troops have died in the Middle East since Operation Epic Fury was launched on Feb. 28 and 868 troops have been wounded, according to the latest Pentagon statistics.
U.S.-Iran Tit-For-Tat Attacks

Meanwhile, the U.S. is continuing to hit Iranian targets in response to what American officials say are threatening actions by Tehran. This includes ongoing Iranian attacks against shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Tuesday, the U.S. carried out its latest airstrikes on Iran’s strategic Qeshm Island in the strait, according to several media accounts.

A U.S. official called the strikes “a defensive response to Iranian forces ‘targeting U.S. personnel and assets’ in the region,” CBS News reported on Wednesday. The U.S. strike was in retaliation for the aforementioned claimed Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain, The Associated Press reported on Wednesday.

The Qeshm Island strike was one of several that went after Iranian coastal targets in recent weeks as friction has increased over U.S. support of ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and growing Iranian frustration with the status quo. The strikes had been carried out largely in secret for several weeks, but the U.S. has become more open to acknowledging them recently.
The timing of the latest U.S. strikes on Qeshm Island “is itself noteworthy,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, pointed out on X.

“Unlike previous U.S. attacks on Iranian coastal areas and islands, which largely took place at night, these strikes were carried out in broad daylight. This could signal a change in the pattern of U.S. military operations against Iran,” Azizi posited.
The U.S. appears to be growing more willing to acknowledge these strikes just as Iran seems to be shifting tactics amid stalled diplomacy.

“Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of deliberate, calibrated escalation,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence service, suggested on X. “The objective is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade.”

“The pattern is increasingly clear: from attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz to attacks on vessels at anchor; from missile strikes to commando operations; and from attacks on U.S. bases in Bahrain to strikes extending into Kuwait, reportedly beginning with drones and progressing to missiles,” he added.

“Initially, Iranian retaliation was framed as a response to direct U.S. attacks,” the analyst continued. “Now, Tehran is increasingly invoking violations of its airspace and sovereignty as grounds for further military action. It potentially expands the range of incidents Iran can use to justify retaliation, creating additional pathways to escalation even without a new direct American strike.”
Supposed Dirty Bomb Threat

On Monday, CNN reported that new U.S. intelligence assessments have indicated that “Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC.”

“Sources familiar with the latest intelligence characterized the Iranian planning as, for now, an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack,” the network added. “But the plotting picked up by the US has been very specific and includes locations and targets, two of the sources said, and has sparked a flurry of US contingency planning.”
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told CNN that the U.S. is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”

But American officials “have viewed the intelligence as a signal of an alarming willingness to escalate by Iran as it faces intense pressure from ongoing US military strikes and a punishing economic blockade that top administration officials have said is ‘devastating’ the country.”
CNN acknowledged that it remains unknown if Iran even has the capability to pull off these kinds of attacks.
TWZ cannot independently verify the reported Iranian dirty bomb threat, which is the latest in a series of dire warnings about actions the Islamic Republic may take against U.S. officials.

“Threats against Americans have ramped up since the start of the ongoing war with Iran,” CBS News noted. “Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in October that Iran has ‘substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel’ abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching ‘advanced stages’ in the Middle East and other countries.”

That Iran would have the interest, let alone be in a position, to set off a dirty bomb in D.C. seems dubious given the response such an attack would provoke from the U.S., as TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway pointed out.

There are a growing number of pundits that are questioning the veracity of all these claims and leaks considering the tough spot the administration is in when it comes to the war it started many months ago.

Still, in response to the dirty bomb claim, President Donald Trump told reporters, “We’re looking into ​it.” Queried about whether there was an imminent threat, Trump said: “Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before.”
Trump added that “we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he did not think there was any imminent threat to the U.S. capital, when asked about the CNN report, Reuters noted.

These latest developments “should serve as an important reminder of the inherent instability of the current situation,” Azizi added. “Some within the Trump administration – and perhaps even Trump himself – may believe that Washington can maintain economic pressure and the naval blockade against Iran indefinitely while avoiding another full-scale war. But the developments of the past 24 hours demonstrate how difficult it is to sustain such an arrangement.”

Earlier this month, Trump declared that “Iran militarily is effectively over,” after meeting Qatari officials in the White House to talk about a peace plan that has so far not gained any real traction. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbors.”

Trump hasn’t shown any overt signs of changing the status quo since he made those comments. For a short period, the U.S. had three aircraft carriers in the CENTCOM region when USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived on Nov. 15, joining the USS George Washington and the USS George H.W. Bush. However, Wednesday afternoon, Bloomberg News reported on X that one of the two flattops on station there had left.
The New York Times reported that the Washington has left the region.
While Trump’s current thinking on whether to launch a new wave of strikes on Iran is unknown, his window to do so may be closing with the Democrats taking control of the Senate and House on Jan. 3.

A day after the Democratic Party’s stunning midterm election victories, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) “said there will be Senate Republican support for ending the war with Iran as soon as possible and threatened that Democrats will use the ‘power of the purse’ to starve the Defense Department of funding if necessary to bring a swift end to the conflict,” The Hill reported.

“We are going to end the war,” Schumer proclaimed. “We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people.”
Given the growing tensions in the region, it remains possible that a much larger conflict could flare up well before the Democrats have a chance to exert their newfound influence.

absaetze.t: Calls to exclude Russia from Venice Architecture Biennale, Public Art Fund announces 2027 program, and more in today's art news.
November 18, 2026 — 3 min read
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.
Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in Closet Breaks Estimates

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.
EU Countries Call to Exclude Russia From Architecture Biennale

Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.
Public Art Fund Announces 2027 Program

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.
More in Today’s News:

Brooklyn artist Julia Jo's "One Fell Swoop" (2026) will be offered at Christie’s evening sale tomorrow, November 19, to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. The New York-based nonprofit has supported unhoused individuals and families in the city through food, clothing, housing, job training, and youth programs since its founding in 1981. "One Fell Swoop" is estimated to fetch between $30,000 and $50,000, though a Christie’s spokesperson told Hyperallergic that “we think it will go for more.”

Two months before the closing of Ana Mendieta at London’s Tate Modern, the Museum of Modern Art has announced it will present the first retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist in the United States in over 20 years.
Leading feminist conceptual artist Eleanor Antin has sued her dealer Richard Saltoun, who operates galleries in New York, London, and Rome, over his alleged withholding of at least 179 works.

After this month’s “blue wave,” President Donald Trump will soon have to contend with a Democrat-majority Congress ready to investigate his culture war tirades against institutions including the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the Kennedy Center.

This week, the City of Sydney in Australia awarded 40 artists $25,000 “no strings attached” grants in a new initiative aimed at preventing the city from losing “its local storytellers and creative soul.”

Five works, including 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and 18th-20th century inscribed crosses, were repatriated to Ethiopia following a ceremony in London today, November 18, as part of a new partnership between the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio and the Ethiopian Heritage Authority.

items.titel: Is My Art Funny to You?
items.anriss: Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that …

absaetze.t: A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.
November 18, 2026 — 5 min read

Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”)

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.
Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

items.titel: Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model
items.anriss: The group Artists 4 Artists Miami is encouraging local artists and arts workers to abstain from the city’s busy week of fairs and think more critically about ways to support the local community year-round

absaetze.t: As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Oorganisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

The campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

And yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”

According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.
“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”

items.titel: Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio among nine new products on Dezeen Showroom
items.anriss: A table lamp comprising a plastic base topped with five magnetically attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.

absaetze.t: A table lamp comprising a plastic base topped with five magnetically attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.
Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio
Magnetic connector points are placed inside the five globe-like bulbs that light this table lamp by Hong Kong-based Canalside Studio.
The Bubbly lamp comprises a statuesque base with five bulbs attached, which can be removed and positioned around a room – including attached to metal surfaces – to spread out its ambient glow.
Other products published last week include a tile collection by Ceramiche Keope, acoustic pods by Actiu and an outdoor rug range by Rima Dain.
Read on to find out about some of our latest products:
Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope
Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope are intended to mimic the striated appearance of natural Villeneuve quartzite quarried in Italy.
As well as being striped with differently coloured striations, the tiles feature the stone’s abundance of mineral inclusions and the glinting mica microcrystals that it is studded with.
Blueroots marble by Antolini
Amber and white veining streaks across the surface of Italian stone company Antolini‘s aptly-named Blueroots marble.
The slabs can be used in kitchens and bathrooms as interior cladding or to create furnishings, imbuing interiors with visually stimulating surfaces.
Qyos acoustic pods by Actiu
Office furniture brand Actiu has evolved its Qyos acoustic pods, expanding on its configuration options and capacity for personalisation.
Described by the brand as “adaptable microarchitecture”, new options include those that enhance both aesthetics and sound absorption.
Palladia tiles by Ceramiche Refin
Italian company Ceramiche Refin‘s latest surface draws on the faceted appearance of traditional terrazzo.
Palladia comes in a trio of colourways – Iride, Luce and Aurea – and a choice of two finishes, glossy Lucida or plain Matt.
New Jetson acoustic pods by Mute
Office brand Mute‘s Jetson acoustic pods have evolved to encompass a wider range of colourways, wall layouts and levels of transparency.

Also enhanced is the pods’ acoustic credentials, which the brand says now meets Class A acoustic standards in accordance with ISO 23351-1, allowing individuals and small groups to work and converse in a quiet environment.
Outdoor rugs by Rima Dain
A range of styles, shapes and sizes are available in the catalogue of Spanish brand Rima Dain, which specialises in outdoor rugs.
Rather than being an afterthought, the rugs aim to help zone and enhance outdoor spaces in both residential and hospitality contexts.
Steel Seal washing machines by Asko
Enhanced and cutting-edge new features aim to make Swedish brand Asko‘s Steel Seal washing machines more seamless, hygienic and pleasant to use.

Two new signature technologies in particular feature in the new machines. Steel Seal, which substitutes rubber components for ones made of steel, and Quattro Construction 2.0, an integrated suspension system that reduces movement and resulting noise when in use.
One Lounge pod layout by Framery
Finnish company Framery has released an internal layout option for its One Pod, featuring a corner sofa in miniature.
One Lounge aims to make users feel at home with the cosy, thickly-padded corner seat, in place of a harder stool.
